The regex.fullmatch method has incorrect behavior when the partial flag is set and the regex uses negative lookahead:

```python
import regex

a = regex.compile(r"(?!(True|False)\b)(.*)")

print(a.fullmatch("True", partial=True))
# Should produce a match (since "True" is a prefix of the match "Truest") but does not.
```

comments.body:
Please clarify.

The comment says "Should produce a match (since "True" is a prefix of the match "Truest") but does not.", but your code is matching against "True", not "Truest".

Are you talking about matching against "True" or "Truest"?

My understanding is that a.fullmatch(b, partial=True) will return a match containing b exactly when b is the prefix of some string that matches a.

In the example codeblock, b="True" is a prefix of many strings that match a (e.g., "Trues", "Truest", "True17"). I expected the output
<regex.Match object; span=(0, 4), match='True'>, but no match was produced.

The regex `True\b` does match the string "True", so `(?!True\b)` doesn't match.

The regex `True\b` doesn't match the string "Truest", so `(?!True\b)` does match.

I agree. "True" does not match the regex a. "Truest" does match the regex a.

Maybe I can better explain my question in code:

```python
import regex
a = regex.compile(r"(?!(True|False)\b)(.*)")


### Behavior we agree on

a.fullmatch("Truest") # "Truest" matches the regex a

a.fullmatch("True") # "True" does not match the regex a

"Truest".startswith("True") # "True" is a prefix of "Truest"

# Therefore, "True" is a prefix of some string that is a fullmatch of a.


### Behavior that confuses me

a.fullmatch("True", **partial = True**) # Does not return a match. Therefore "True" is **not** a prefix of some string that is a fullmatch of a.
```


If this is the intended behavior, then I am not understanding what partial = True is supposed to do. Can you explain the intended behavior of partial = True?
"True" is not a prefix because you're explicitly rejecting any string that starts with "True" followed by a word boundary, and the end of the string is a word boundary.

Thank you, I think I understand your point now. You are saying that, when `a.fullmatch("True", partial=True)` runs, "True" matches `(?!True/b)`  because the end of the string is treated as a word boundary.

I can understand how this makes sense in the implementation. However, I don't think it makes sense semantically. 

When I run `a.fullmatch("True", partial=True)`, I am asking if there exists any string matching the regex `True.*` that also matches the regex `a`. Of course, there are many such strings (e.g., "Truest"). 
Although it makes sense to treat the end of string as a word boundary when partial=False, the end of the string should not be treated as a word boundary when partial=True. Because the input string ("True") is interpreted a prefix, there may not actually be a word boundary after "True" in its completions (e.g., like "Truest").

It seems to me that the stored matching text for back references probably doesn't _need_ to be discovered within the text being searched.

And I have a use case where I want to do half a match, and then finish the match against a variety of other candidate strings, but with the caveat that backreferences contained in the second part see into the first part. 

Naively I might just run the full regex against a variety of different concatenations in all their permutations, but that seems inefficient. 

Alternatively, I can match the front half once and then copy the groups into a simplified prefix on the regex and the format string, which is also pretty inefficient but potentially simpler than the original expression.

Something like this but cleaner and more efficient:
```python
def rematch(pattern, string, **kwargs):
    unique = "ZaYbXcWdvEuF"
    initlist = [ f"{k}='(?P<{k}>.*)'" for k in kwargs.keys() ]
    pattern = f"{', '.join(initlist)}:{unique}:" + pattern
    initlist = [ f"{k}='{v}'" for k, v in kwargs.items() ]
    string = f"{', '.join(initlist)}:{unique}:" + string return re.match(pattern, string) 
```

Or... just rewrite the regex with the discovered backreferences cooked in and recompile that.

Would it be feasible to just pass in the initial state of backreference groups to the match function so they don't have to be embedded in the string being searched and the regex doesn't have to be recompiled every time?
title: Pre-initialisation of back references

body:
Consider the following code:

```python
import re
import regex

print(re.match(r'\w', '²'))
print(regex.match(r'\w', '²'))
```

This prints:

```
<re.Match object; span=(0, 1), match='²'>
None
```
`re` is considering `'²'` to be a word character, and `regex` is not.

This doesn't change if I pass a `UNICODE` flag to both.

The `re` docs say:

> \w
>
> For Unicode (str) patterns:
>
> Matches Unicode word characters; this includes all Unicode alphanumeric characters (as defined by [str.isalnum()](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.isalnum)), as well as the underscore (_).

`'²'.isalnum()` does indeed return true, and it's in the `No` unicode category (other numbers) so should presumably count as numeric. So I think this is an example where `re` is doing the right thing and `regex` is doing the wrong thing.

I tested this on Python 3.12.9, running `regex==2024.11.6`, on Linux.

comments.body:
According to the Unicode docs at https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr18/, the definition of `\w` is `[\p{alpha}\p{gc=Mark}\p{digit}\p{gc=Connector_Punctuation}\p{Join_Control}]`.

The definition of `\p{digit}` is `\p{gc=Decimal_Number}`, which does not include `'\xB2'` (`'²'`).

Unicode rules I believe restrict the numerical matching to the "Decimal Number" (`Nd`) category. So, something like this being equivalent to word per the [Unicode spec](https://unicode.org/reports/tr18/#Compatibility_Properties).

```py
>>> regex.match(r'[\p{alnum}\p{M}\p{Pc}\p{JoinControl}]', '²')
>>>
```

If you use something that captures all numbers (`N`), only then would you capture the 2 in this case.

```py
>>> regex.match(r'[\p{L}\p{N}\p{M}\p{Pc}\p{JoinControl}]', '²')
<regex.Match object; span=(0, 1), match='²'>
```

I assume this is because Regex implements "word" rules according the spec, at the very least, I assume they are using the `Nd` category which will not include such numbers. Various implementations of regular expression engines seem to vary on what is considered a "word" character. Some, for instance, implement `\w` as `[\p{L}\p{N}_]`. It's possible Python's `re` is doing something similar.

Fair enough! Well, I withdraw the implicit claim that `regex` is in error according to the spec, but the `re` module documents its behaviour here quite clearly and is unlikely to change it, so it's a place where `regex` isn't backwards compatible with `re` either way.

title: Discrepancy from re module on what unicode characters are considered words

For the [lark](https://github.com/lark-parser/lark) parsing library we use the (sadly private) stdlib `re._parser` library to query the minimum and maximum length of a regex:

https://github.com/lark-parser/lark/blob/942366b49247e996e387cb901ed96c7d861382a0/lark/utils.py#L132-L156

As can be seen from the snippet, since we also support using `regex` instead of `re`, we need to take special care when encountering regex specific syntax, like nested sets category patterns. The only value that needs to be correct is if minimum length is 0 or greater since we depend on Regular Expressions being non-empty in a few places.

It would be nice if there was a way a query the minimum and maximum match size from a compiled regex object. The stdlib re module is lower priority since there there is at least a way to accesses this information reliably, but I am probably also going to make a request there.

comments.body: Does you expect the minimum and maximum to be accurate? That would be difficult if there were references to capture groups or calls.

accurate in the sense that all possible matches will fall into this range, even if no match with that length actually exists, yes. And preferably of-course the 0/1+ distinction of min should be fully accurate.

Currently, only the `_cache` variable has a threading lock, and it's only used for write operations. All global variables need to use a lock for both read and write accesses.

In order to be thread safe, values which have the possibility of being changed in one thread and which can be either read or written from another thread need to be protected by a threading lock prior to either reading or writing them. If they are protected only upon writing, then they can be read while the writing thread is in the middle of a write, which can result in undefined operation. While it would be possible to design Python such that a lock isn't needed upon read, Python isn't designed that way, and it's definitely not something which is guaranteed. Not needing a lock upon read accesses would only be possible if changes to every readable value were always something accomplished with a single memory write access. That's just not the case in Python. So, for thread safety, locks need to be obtained prior to both read and write operations from/to variables which are accessible to more than one thread (i.e. basically any value which isn't local to a function).

Specifically, every access to `_cache` needs to be protected by the `_cache_lock` `RLock` which is currently used only for writes. In addition, all other global variables need to use thread locking semantics for both reading and writing.

Ideally, *everything* which can, potentially, be changed and accessed by multiple threads should be protected by a lock of some sort (`RLock()` is normally  good). You don't need to lock things like constants, which are never changed once initially set upon package initialization, but things like `_named_args`, `_replacement_cache`, `_locale_sensitive`, and even `_cache_all`, and any other global settings, should only be accessed (read or write) once a threading lock has been obtained. A potential alternative for some variables would be to use a value which is only accessible to the current thread.

I don't have a specific thread safety test cases for the regex package, but I have tested thread safety with only obtaining locks for writes, but not reads, in other Python code and experienced issues.
title: Thread safety: need lock for both read and write (_cache and other global variables)

In [1]: regex.search(r'(voices){1i+1d+2s<=2}', 'voixes voicees', regex.BESTMATCH)

**[Original report](https://bitbucket.org/mrabarnett/mrab-regex/issue/425) by Anonymous.**

----------------------------------------

Attemting to match `BUG!` with the following regex causes the named group `<bug>` to store the value of the numbered group `\1`.

```
(?|(?P<bug>xxx)(!)
  |(?P<bug>BUG)(!)
)
```

=> `<bug>` will contain `!` instead of `BUG`

A second bug can be seen when we change the regex to not redefine `<bug>`; then, the numbered group `\1` gets dropped alltogether.

A file with test cases are attached.

Mixing named and numbered groups is probably not done intentionally by most people (although i guess there could be applications for it), but by accidentally omitting the non-capturing `(?:)` boilerplate.

comments.body:
**Original comment by Matthew Barnett (Bitbucket: [mrabarnett](https://bitbucket.org/mrabarnett), GitHub: [mrabarnett](https://github.com/mrabarnett)).**

----------------------------------------

That's an interesting issue, but is it a bug?

The rule is that groups are numbered consecutively 1, 2, 3, etc, but named groups have the same group number.

The problem here is that the branch reset is restarting the numbering and it's not skipping over group numbers that have already been used in that branch. The question is whether it should.

To give another example, if the second branch was `(BUG)(?<bug>!)`, then, according to the rule, `(BUG)` would be group 1 because it's the first group in the branch and `(?<bug>!)` would also be group 1 because it's a named group that’s already defined as group 1.

I'll need to see how other implementations handle the question.

**Original comment by Matthew Barnett (Bitbucket: [mrabarnett](https://bitbucket.org/mrabarnett), GitHub: [mrabarnett](https://github.com/mrabarnett)).**

----------------------------------------

re: Compiled patterns have a `groupindex` attribute that maps group names to group numbers, so a group name can be linked to only 1 group number. This must also be true of regex in order to maintain compatibility. Branch reset is not supported..

Perl: Both branches of a branch reset number consecutively, and a group name can be linked to more than 1 group number. This behaviour is incompatible with `re`, and therefore `regex`.

PCRE2: Both branches of a branch reset will number consecutively, but group number can be linked to only 1 group name, so a pattern such as `(?|(?<AA>aa)|(?<BB>bb))` will cause an error.

C#: Unnamed groups are numbered first, followed by named groups. This behaviour different from `re`, and therefore `regex`. Branch reset is not supported.

So, what should the rule be? How should group numbers be assigned in the examples below?

```
(?|(?P<bug>xxx)(!)|(?P<bug>BUG)(!))  (currently 1, 2, 1, 1)
(?|(?P<bug>xxx)(!)|(BUG)(?P<bug>!))  (currently 1, 2, 1, 1)
(?|(xxx)(?P<bug>!)|(?P<bug>BUG)(!))  (currently 1, 2, 2, 1)
(?|(xxx)(?P<bug>!)|(BUG)(?P<bug>!))  (currently 1, 2, 1, 2)
```

Some options are:

1. Number consecutively \(current behaviour\).
2. Number consecutively, but skip group numbers that have been used up to that point in the branch.
3. Number consecutively, but skip group numbers that have used anywhere in that branch.

‌

According to Regex's documentation, when given just a property name (or short name), the order of evaluation is: General Category, Script, Block, and Binary properties. There is no bug here and it seems Regex does exactly what it states, but while it operates as intended, I wonder if this is incorrect compared to Perl implementation which I assume inspired this feature and its behavior (at least generally).

It appears in Perl, Binary properties take priority over Script and Block which makes sense (to me) as Binary really only has one form to specify properties `p\{name}` while script and blocks have two `\p{blk=name}`/`\p{sc=name}` as well as `\p{name}`.

Consider the Perl Unicode property documentation in regards to the block alias of `IDC`:

```
\p{Block: Ideographic_Description_Characters} (Short: \p{Blk=IDC};
                            NOT \p{ID_Continue} NOR \p{Is_IDC}) (16:
                            U+2FF0..2FFF)
```

 And note the Binary property that also shares that alias of `IDC`:

```
\p{ID_Continue: Y*}     (Short: \p{IDC=Y}, \p{IDC}) (134_434:
                            [0-9A-Z_a-z\xaa\xb5\xb7\xba\xc0-\xd6
                            \xd8-\xf6\xf8-\xff], U+0100..02C1,
                            U+02C6..02D1, U+02E0..02E4, U+02EC,
                            U+02EE ...)
```

The binary property seems to take priority when it comes to the alias of `IDC`, but in Regex, it does not:

```py
>>> regex.match(r'\p{idc}', '\u3005')
>>> regex.match(r'\p{id_continue}', '\u3005')
<regex.Match object; span=(0, 1), match='々'>
```

I'm not sure if this is just a purposeful deviation from Perl? Or Perl has since changed its approach since Regex modeled it after this? Or if Regex is not concerned with how Perl actually does this.

On a side note, it also seems that seems Regex treats short names of scripts as `script` instead of `script_extensions` like Perl does, which also may be something that Regex is purposefully doing, or maybe wasn't aware that had changed in Perl. It seems Perl thinks that `script_extensions` is generally more useful a result for this than `script` which was why the change occurred.

 Interested to hear your opinion on these.

comments.body:
**Original comment by Matthew Barnett (Bitbucket: [mrabarnett](https://bitbucket.org/mrabarnett), GitHub: [mrabarnett](https://github.com/mrabarnett)).**

----------------------------------------

The problem with much of regex \(as in “regular expression”\) is that there has never been a definitive implementation or explanation about how things should behave. Perl added much, but others did their own thing, and details can change over time.

For example, PCRE \(Perl-Compatible …\) has `\p{Greek}` equivalent to `\p{Script=Greek}`, presumably because that’s what Perl did at the time, but, as you point out, Perl now has `\p{Greek}` equivalent to `\p{Script_Extensions=Greek}`.

If I \(or PCRE\) change it, it could break code.

What do other implementations do?

**Original comment by Isaac Muse (Bitbucket: [facelessuser](https://bitbucket.org/facelessuser), GitHub: [facelessuser](https://github.com/facelessuser)).**

----------------------------------------

‌

> If I \(or PCRE\) change it, it could break code.
>
> What do other implementations do?

I’m not certain as of right now. 

Interestingly, Perl now discourages representing `block` as `\p{name}` and `\p{in_name}`. [https://perldoc.perl.org/perluniprops#Discouraged](https://perldoc.perl.org/perluniprops#Discouraged). It seems they got lucky for a long time and have now realized that The _**Unicode Consortium**_ isn’t trying to keep block names or aliases unique from scripts or even general category. They seem to mention `Is_*` properties under discouraged, though don’t actually mark them in their list with the `X` which signifies discouragement. They seem to mainly be focusing on encouraging people to start specifying `block` as `block=name` or `blk=name` as block seems to be the cause of all the conflicts \(or better put, doing this with block removes all the current conflicts\).

I will also backtrack and say that one can specify binary properties in more than one way as well which I imagine removes conflict: `\p{BinaryName}` or `\p{BinaryName: true}`.

Anyways, I don’t necessarily have a solution and was more curious if Regex was aware of these changes, and if so what the stance on this was.

**Original comment by Isaac Muse (Bitbucket: [facelessuser](https://bitbucket.org/facelessuser), GitHub: [facelessuser](https://github.com/facelessuser)).**

----------------------------------------

As far as `script` vs `script_extensions` go, just looking at `pcre2test`, it appears they still use `script` as they find the first character, which is in `script`, but does not find the character in `script_extensions`. This is using Unicode 13.

```
PCRE2 version 10.35 2020-05-09
  re> /\p{Latin}/g
data> \x{2b8}\x{363}
 0: \x{2b8}
data>
```

After digging a little more, I do also realize there is a difference between PCRE vs Perl, where PCRE is inspired by Perl, it is not guaranteed to match Perl.

So maybe there is no issue here at all. I think maybe I assumed this was matching Perl closer as it allows a lot of Unicode properties in a very Perlish way \(such as `is_` and `in_`\). But it sounds like this leans more towards PCRE.

While there aren’t a lot of conflicts, there are some, and I think in the end, it can be noted that using explicit patterns such as `\p{blk=name}`, `\p{sc=name}` \(or `\p{scx=name}`\) and `\p{name=t}` is the safest way to ensure you get what you want, especially if you intend to target a binary or block property in regex.

Firstly, why do you have `re.S` instead of `regex.S`?

Secondly, your patterns have small differences between them, and the third one isn't valid as written \("unbalanced parenthesis at position 35"\).

Thirdly, if you don't put the subpatterns in a DEFINE group then it'll try to match them, so just removing the enclosing `DEFINE` will result in a different behaviour.

Finally, `(?P<e>[cd]|(?&e))` is a nasty pattern because if it can't match `[cd]` it’ll just call itself, leading to infinite recursion.

Recursion is something that was added to regexes by, I believe, Perl, but it's a not a good fit. There are better tools such as `pyparsing` for that kind of thing.

So I suspect that it’s a infinite recursion that’s causing the MemoryError.

**[Original report](https://bitbucket.org/mrabarnett/mrab-regex/issue/367) by Anonymous.**

----------------------------------------

`(?!(1{2,})\1+$)((?:11)+)$` should match only strings consisting of n '1's, where n is an even prime. But, best I can tell, this returns a partial match for all n greater than 2:

```
regex.match(r'(?!(1{2,})\1+$)((?:11)+)$', '1' * n, partial=True)
```

which implies that there is some n that would yield a full match, and thus a second even prime.

We can also see that there exists a number greater than 2 which is an integer power of both 2 and 3:

```
>>> regex.match(r'(?=(?P<po2>1$|(?P<sd2>1+)(?=\g<sd2>$)(?&po2)$))(?P<po3>1$|(?P<sd3>1+)\g<sd3>(?=\g<sd3>)(?&po3)$)', '11', partial=True)
<regex.Match object; span=(0, 2), match='11', partial=True>
```

Less sensationally, this also gives a partial match:

```
regex.match(r'(?!.+).*', '1', partial=True)
```

So I guess the problem is that partial matching assumes lookaheads are satisfiable. But, as the sillier examples show, it's not enough to consider them independently; you can always add ones to get a prime number or an even number, just not both at the same time.

I don't expect this regex engine to solve every number theory problem that can be expressed in this regexp dialect (though it'd be pretty cool if that turned out to be possible). But the limitations should probably be documented somewhere.
title: regex thinks there's a second even prime

You also need to remember that it doesn't check every time around the loop because that would slow it down too much, so if the check occurs just before the maximum time, it might not check again until the replacement function has returned, which, in the example, would be almost 0.5 seconds after the maximum time. This won't be such a problem if it's just matching and is 'merely' suffering from catastrophic backtracking.

**Original comment by Isaac Muse (Bitbucket: [facelessuser](https://bitbucket.org/facelessuser), GitHub: [facelessuser](https://github.com/facelessuser)).**

It seems that a busy wait does work, for the most part:

```py
from time import time
import regex


def slow_replace(m):
    start = time()
    while True:
        elapsed = time() - start
        if elapsed >= 0.5:
            print(elapsed)
            break
    return 'X'

regex.sub(r'[a-z]', slow_replace, 'abcde', timeout=2)
```

This doesn't seem to throw the timeout even though it is technically over 2 seconds. I assume this is just related to timing of when the delta is checked. I imagine by time it is checking the operation, is already finished, even though it technically exceeded the time limit.

0.5

I think the problem is that Windows is measuring "wall" time, whereas macOS is measuring processor time. The 'sleep' function doesn't consume any processor time, so macOS isn't seeing 'slow_replace' as a slow function.

In practice, though, Python _will_ be consuming processor time, busily matching (or whatever), so I don't think it's really a problem.

You can test that by replacing the 'sleep' function with a busy wait.

Sometimes you're going to get long runtimes due to backtracking.

Sometimes it's easy to see that a regex won't match in a certain position, so it can short-circuit, which is what's happening in the first example, but other times it's not so easy.

It's all a question of how much effort should be expended to look for a shortcut.

You might say that it wouldn't take much more effort to spot a shortcut in the second example, or the third example, but at each step, someone will be able to provide another example that would need only a little bit more difficult than the last, and this could go on indefinitely!

And there's already a _lot_ of code in the module...

I just found a chapter in the Unicode guidelines for regular expressions concerning property values and would like to ask, whether supporting of regex patterns (or some subset thereof) here would be possible.
http://unicode.org/reports/tr18/#Wildcard_Properties

I am not aware of any implementation already supporting it, nor do I know how much extra complexity for the parser would be needed, but it looks like a feature orthogonal with unicode properties and the set operations which regex already has.

I see, that the usecases would cover rather special approaches - in my case it would allow for investigating the unicode character repertoire itself (Currently I can do something like that after grabbing all the character names via unicodedata).

Otherwise, on "normal" text, the cases could be covered, where there are multiple character ranges, that should be considered (i.e. basic xxx, xxx supplement, xxx extended ...). (I am not sure how the current Script property relates to this exactly.) 
E.g. some errors or even spoofing attempts might be checked for on graphically similar characters from different ranges. cf.

* (dec: 111; hex: 0x6f) LATIN SMALL LETTER O
* (dec: 959; hex: 0x3bf) GREEK SMALL LETTER OMICRON
* (dec: 1086; hex: 0x43e) CYRILLIC SMALL LETTER O
* (dec: 1413; hex: 0x585) ARMENIAN SMALL LETTER OH

I'd like to stress, that this is only meant as proposal for consideration - it surely wouldn't be worth some extensive effort or the risk for being possible bug source.
